title: Redundant Connection
statement: A tree with n nodes labelled 1..n has exactly n-1 edges and no cycle. You are given a graph that started as such a tree, with one extra edge added between two existing nodes — so it has n nodes and n edges, and exactly one cycle. Return the edge that can be removed to leave a tree. If more than one answer exists, return the one that appears last in the input.
realWorld: Network topology validation: a switch fabric is meant to be loop-free, and one miscabled link creates a broadcast storm. The link to disable is the one that closed the loop — the last cable added between two segments that could already reach each other. Spanning tree protocols solve exactly this.

examples.explanation: After [1,2] and [1,3], nodes 2 and 3 already reach each other through 1. The edge [2,3] closes the cycle, so removing it leaves a tree.
The cycle is 1-2-3-4-1. Processing in order, [1,4] is the first edge whose endpoints are already connected, and it is the last edge of the cycle in input order.

constraints: ai != bi, there are no repeated edges, and the graph is connected

complexity.space: O(n) for the rebuilt adjacency list and the visited array

bruteForce.whySlow: Every candidate removal rebuilds the graph and re-runs a full traversal, so n traversals of O(n) work each. Worse, it asks a whole-graph question ('is this still a tree?') to learn something local: whether one edge joins two nodes that were already connected.

patternIdentification: The edge to remove is the one whose endpoints could already reach each other before it was added. That is a connectivity question over edges arriving in order, with no interest in the path — the definition of union-find. Process the edges left to right; the first `union` that finds both endpoints already sharing a root is the answer, and because there is exactly one cycle, that first failure is also the last cycle edge in input order.

optimized.idea: Union the endpoints of each edge in input order. A union whose two endpoints already share a root adds nothing — the nodes were connected by an earlier path, so this edge closes the cycle. Return it immediately. The union that does nothing is the answer.

commonMistakes: Sizing the arrays as `new int[n]` when nodes are labelled 1..n — index n is then out of bounds. Allocate n+1 and ignore slot 0.

Returning the first edge of the cycle rather than the edge that closed it. Processing in input order and returning on the first failed union gives the last-appearing edge automatically; no extra bookkeeping is needed.
Collecting every edge that fails the union and returning the last one. With exactly one extra edge there is only ever one failure, and scanning on wastes the early exit.

Applying this to a *directed* graph problem such as Redundant Connection II. Union-find has no notion of direction, so it cannot tell a node with two parents from a genuine cycle; that variant needs a separate parent check first.
Unioning the nodes instead of their roots (`parent[b] = a`), which detaches b's existing subtree and silently corrupts later queries.
